unit.title: Perform testing and inspection of electrical installations

summary: This unit teaches you to verify that an electrical installation is safe and follows the Jamaican code, which is based on the NEC (NFPA 70): to plan and lead the inspection and testing of new work (initial verification) and of existing installations, to carry out the dead tests, to check everything before the supply is energised, to interpret the live test results a competent person provides, to test GFCI and AFCI devices, to record defects, and to complete the test record and reports. You will also learn how the Government Electrical Regulator's inspection and approval lead to a JPS connection, and how to supervise trainees doing the testing.

blocks.p: An installation that looks finished is not safe until it has been **inspected and tested**. Inspection finds what the eye can see: wrong conductor sizes, missing covers, unsuitable fittings, missing bonding. Testing finds what the eye cannot: a broken grounding conductor, failing insulation, reversed polarity, a ground-fault path too weak for the breaker to trip fast. At Level 3 you plan the verification, lead the team, judge the results and sign the paperwork. (This kit builds on EEMINS0022B, the Level 2 unit on basic testing; it goes further into planning, calculations, inspection of existing installations, defect reporting and approval.)

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the verification
Collect the approved drawings, panel schedules and design data; agree access, shutdowns and limitations with the client; choose the team and the instruments.
Work safely
Isolate, lock off and prove dead; warn others before tests that put voltage on conductors; keep live tests for a competent person.
Inspect against the NEC and the drawings
Check the installation against the approved drawings, the NEC rules the Centre uses and the inspection checklist, and record what you find.
Carry out the dead tests
Continuity of grounding and bonding conductors, insulation resistance, polarity and ground electrode resistance, in the right order and with the right instrument.
Do the calculations
Loop resistance from cable data, expected loop impedance and ground-fault current, voltage drop, and parallel insulation readings.
Verify before energising
Confirm that the dead tests are complete and recorded, covers are on, loads are off and everyone is clear before a competent person energises.
Test GFCI and AFCI devices
Use the TEST button and a plug-in tester, and know what the results mean.
Inspect existing installations
Agree extent and limitations, sample, find deterioration and bad alterations, and record each defect by seriousness.
Record and report
Test records, panel schedules, defect reports and inspection reports, correctly signed.
Hand over and advise
Explain the results, show the client the TEST buttons, support the GER inspection and JPS connection, and deal with refusals.
Lead and supervise
Give roles, check instruments and method, question odd results and retest samples yourself.

ul: The supply from JPS to homes and most businesses is **110/220 V, single-phase, three-wire, 50 Hz**: two hot conductors and a neutral. Either hot conductor to neutral is **110 V**; the two hot conductors together give **220 V**. Larger premises have three-phase supplies. Plugs and receptacles are **US-style**.

Jamaica's electrical code follows the US **National Electrical Code (NEC, NFPA 70)**. You inspect against the NEC and the **approved drawings**, with GFCI and AFCI protection, grounding and bonding as the NEC requires. Your instructor will tell you which edition the Government Electrical Regulator has adopted: the rules for GFCI and AFCI areas change from edition to edition.

The **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)** replaced the Government Electrical Inspectorate under the Electricity Act 2015. A new or altered installation is inspected, and the inspection is certified by a licensed inspector, before **JPS** will connect it. Your own verification is done first, so the installation is ready when the inspector arrives. Confirm the current procedure and forms with your instructor.
Conductor sizes are in **AWG** (American wire gauge). This kit gives the metric equivalent in mm² beside each size. The metric figure is approximate: use the data for the cable actually installed.
The climate and buildings matter: salt air, sun, heavy rain, hurricanes, hollow block walls, termites and rats all leave their marks on an installation.

blocks.note: Even where a job is 'only a small addition', the GER's rules and JPS's rules still apply. Never tell a client that an inspection can be skipped. If you are not sure whether a job needs inspection, ask the GER or your instructor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: The **approved drawings** and the **panel schedule**: each circuit's number, what it feeds, conductor type and size (AWG), length, breaker type and rating, GFCI and AFCI details.

Design data: the load calculation, the expected loop impedance at the service, the trip current of each breaker from the maker's data, cable resistance data (mΩ per metre), the grounding arrangement and the sizes of the bonding jumpers.
The specification (it may set test voltages, limits and margins) and the maker's instructions for special equipment (surge protective devices, drives, generators, solar PV).
For an existing installation: any earlier report, records of alterations, and what the client knows about problems.
Who is on site, what must stay on, and when circuits can be switched off.

blocks.p: Give each person a role: lead inspector, inspector, tester and recorder, and swap roles so everyone tests. Check every instrument before the job:

Continuity of grounding and bonding conductors

Insulation at 250 V, 500 V or 1 000 V DC
Reads OL open and near zero shorted; leads in good order

Wiring faults and GFCI trip at receptacles

flow: Plan and agree with the client
Safe isolation: switch off, lock off, tag, prove the tester, prove dead, prove the tester
Inspection against the NEC and the approved drawings
Dead tests: continuity of grounding and bonding conductors, insulation resistance, polarity, ground electrode
A competent person energises, and does the live tests: voltage at the service, loop impedance, GFCI and AFCI tests, phase rotation (three-phase)
Records, defect report, handover and the GER inspection

blocks.p: The order matters. Continuity first, so you know the grounding conductor is there before you rely on it. Insulation before energising, so a short or ground fault is found before power is applied. Live tests last, and only by a competent person.

blocks.note: An insulation tester puts up to 1 000 V on the conductors. Warn everyone, make sure nobody is touching the circuit at the far end, and let the cables discharge before you touch them. Disconnect electronic equipment, LED drivers, dimmers, surge protective devices and the electronics of GFCI and AFCI devices first (or follow the maker's test instructions): the test can destroy them and they make the reading false.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: In a working supermarket, clinic, office or hotel, circuits feed freezers, tills, computers, medical equipment and guests. Agree with the manager when each circuit can be switched off, how long for, and what must be done first (save data, move stock, use standby supplies). Write it down. For an existing installation, this agreement is part of the **extent and limitations**.

ul: Brief the team on the drawings, the order of work and the safety rules before you start.
Check their instruments, leads and nulling first.
Watch the method on the first circuits and correct mistakes early.
Compare readings with what you expect: longer circuits give higher loop resistance; similar circuits give similar readings. Readings that are all the same, or too neat, are a warning sign.
Retest a sample yourself, and sign the record only when you are satisfied.
Live tests are done only by you or another competent person.

blocks.p: The inspection is done with the installation isolated, before any test, using your eyes, a torch and a screwdriver, against the **approved drawings**, the **NEC rules the Centre uses** and the inspection checklist. It finds more defects than all the tests together. Some defects can be found only by inspection: a fitting not listed for a wet location, a missing filler plate in a panel, a cable too close to a hot pipe, a missing label.

head: Area
Check
Why it matters
rows: Service and grounding
Service entrance, main disconnect, grounding electrode (or electrodes) and its conductor, the main bonding jumper in the service equipment, neutral and ground joined at the service only
The whole fault protection depends on the grounding and bonding
Bonding

Bonding of metal water piping, gas piping as the NEC and the gas supplier require, and structural steel; conductors of the size the NEC table gives; listed clamps on clean metal, close to where the pipe enters
Keeps metal parts at the same voltage in a fault
Panels

Right type and rating of every breaker; no empty spaces without filler plates; covers on; neat, tight terminations; a panel directory; neutral and ground bars separate in sub-panels; no two conductors under one breaker screw unless it is made for it; a dual-supply warning where a generator or PV system is connected
Fingers and tools must not reach live parts; users must know what each breaker feeds
Conductor size against breaker
The breaker rating must not exceed what the conductor can carry. For small conductors the NEC limits are 14 AWG (2.1 mm²) to 15 A, 12 AWG (3.3 mm²) to 20 A and 10 AWG (5.3 mm²) to 30 A
A breaker larger than the conductor can carry lets it overheat
Cable routes and support
Cables and conduit supported, protected where they could be damaged, not touching hot pipes, kept apart from data cables, not resting on ceiling tiles
Damage and overheating
Fire-stopping
Openings where cables pass through fire-rated walls and floors sealed with an approved fire-stopping material
Stops fire and smoke spreading
Outdoor and wet locations
Fittings listed for wet or damp locations; weather-resistant receptacles with in-use covers outdoors; UV-resistant conduit; sealed connectors and drain holes
Water entry causes faults and shocks
GFCI and AFCI protection

GFCI where the NEC edition in use requires it: bathrooms, kitchen counters, outdoors, garages, laundry areas, near sinks and pool areas. AFCI protection in dwelling areas such as bedrooms and living rooms, as the edition requires
Shock risk is highest where people are wet; arcing at damaged wiring starts fires
Receptacles and switches

Secure, undamaged, correctly polarised, ground terminal connected; switches in the hot conductor, never in the neutral; 15 A and 20 A receptacles matching their circuits; 220 V receptacles of the right shape for the load
A switch in the neutral leaves the fitting live when 'off'
Terminations
A sample checked for tightness; no bare copper showing beyond the terminal; no strands cut off
Loose terminals overheat and arc
Equipment

Disconnects in sight of motors and air-conditioning units; overload settings from the nameplate (about 115% to 125% of nameplate current for most motors, within what the NEC and maker allow); guards and covers fitted
Safe maintenance and correct protection
Standby supplies
Transfer switch that cannot connect generator and mains together; no 'plug on both ends' lead; generator grounded as designed and placed outdoors; labels
Back-feed into JPS lines can kill a line worker
Labels and notices
Panel directory, GFCI and AFCI test notice, warning labels
Users and the next inspector need them

blocks.p: The NEC and US-made equipment use **NEMA enclosure types** and the words 'damp location' and 'wet location'. Type 1 is for indoors. **Type 3R** is rainproof and suits most outdoor panels and boxes. **Type 4** is watertight and hose-proof. **Type 4X** adds protection against corrosion, which suits coastal sites. Imported equipment may carry an **IP rating** instead. IP ratings have two digits: the first (0–6) is protection against solids and dust, the second (0–8) against water. An **IP65** fitting is dust-tight and resists water jets; an IP20 fitting keeps fingers out but has no water protection, so it is for indoors only. The two systems do not match exactly: use the maker's data and the location the fitting is listed for.

head: Sign
Common cause in Jamaica
rows: Rust and green corrosion on boxes, clamps and terminals
Salt air near the coast; damp
Brittle, cracked or faded plastic
Sun on outdoor conduit, cables and fittings that are not UV-resistant
Water marks, mud lines, rust inside low boxes
Flooding; heavy rain entering outdoor boxes
Gnawed cables, nests, insect debris
Rats and termites in roof spaces
Heat marks, discoloured terminals, a burnt smell
Loose connections; overloading
Extra circuits, air-conditioning units and receptacles with no change to the supply or panel
Alterations made without design
Brittle insulation, cloth or rubber cables, no GFCI protection
Age

blocks.note: Write every observation as you find it: **what** it is, **where** it is, and the **action** needed. 'Loose terminal, neutral of circuit 7, kitchen panel, remake' can be acted on; 'wiring poor' cannot.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The NEC sets the installation rules; it does not give a list of test limits. The limits you use come from the specification, the instrument maker and good practice, and the Centre's instructor tells you which to follow.

blocks.h: 1. Continuity of grounding and bonding conductors

blocks.p: Null the leads of the low-resistance ohmmeter first. Then test:

ul: **Bonding conductors and the main bonding jumper**: from the ground bar at the service to each bonding clamp. Expect a very low reading, usually well below 0.1 Ω for a short conductor; it must be low and steady.

**The equipment grounding conductor (EGC) of each circuit**, by the **loop method**: link the hot conductor and the EGC together at the panel, then measure between hot and ground at every point on the circuit. The reading at the far end is the **loop resistance**: the resistance of the hot conductor plus the EGC. Record the highest reading. This method also proves that each outlet has its ground connected.

**Neutral and ground in a sub-panel**: with the feeder isolated, the neutral bar and the ground bar should read **open**. A reading means the neutral is bonded to ground in the wrong place: current then flows on the grounding conductors, and GFCIs trip for no reason. The neutral is joined to ground at the service only.

blocks.p: Cable data gives the resistance of the hot conductor plus the EGC in **milliohms per metre (mΩ/m)** at about 20 °C. **Expected loop resistance = length × mΩ/m ÷ 1 000.** Example: a 28 m circuit of 10 AWG pairs at 6.6 mΩ/m would read 28 × 6.6 = 184.8 mΩ, about **0.18 Ω**. A measured value close to the expected one is right; one much higher points to a loose joint, a damaged conductor or a longer route than the drawing shows; one much lower suggests a parallel path (for example through metal conduit) or a short length. Copper resistance rises about 4% for every 10 °C, so a reading in a hot roof space is higher than the table.

head: Hot conductor + EGC, same size, copper
Size in mm² (approx.)
Typical loop resistance (mΩ per metre at 20 °C)
rows: 14 AWG + 14 AWG
About 16.6
12 AWG + 12 AWG
About 10.4
10 AWG + 10 AWG
About 6.6
8 AWG + 8 AWG
About 4.1
6 AWG + 6 AWG

blocks.p: Use the figures the Centre or the cable maker gives you: these are typical values for copper conductors of the same size. Where the EGC is smaller than the hot conductor, as the NEC allows on larger circuits, add the two resistances separately: the EGC part is higher per metre.

**Typical practice** on 110/220 V circuits is to test at **500 V DC** with a megger, and to look for **1 MΩ or more**. The NEC does not set the figure, and many specifications ask for much more, so follow the specification and the Centre's instructor. Extra-low-voltage circuits and electronics need a lower test voltage or must be disconnected: follow the maker.

ul: Isolate, prove dead, switch all switches on and remove lamps, or disconnect lamps, drivers, electronics and surge protective devices (or follow the maker's test instructions).
On a 110/220 V circuit, test **between every pair of conductors**: each hot to neutral, hot to hot, and each conductor to ground (or all live conductors joined together, to ground).
Hold the test until the reading settles. Record the lowest reading for each circuit.
A new installation should read far above 1 MΩ, usually hundreds of megohms or OL. A reading between 1 and 2 MΩ passes the usual limit but should be investigated.
After the test, let the circuit discharge before touching it.

blocks.p: **Circuits in parallel.** Insulation resistances combine like resistors in parallel, so the reading for a whole panel is **lower** than any single circuit. Two circuits of 400 MΩ each read about 200 MΩ together; four circuits of 80 MΩ each read about 20 MΩ. If the whole panel reads lower than the limit, test each circuit alone to find the low one. A low reading on the whole panel is **not** in itself a fault, but one very low circuit pulls the total down towards its own value.

Confirm with continuity tests, before energising, that: every single-pole switch and every breaker is in the **hot** conductor; the centre contact of a screw lampholder is connected to the hot conductor and the screw shell to the neutral; and receptacles are wired with the hot conductor on the **brass** terminal (the narrow slot), the neutral on the **silver** terminal (the wide slot) and the ground on the green screw. After energising, a plug-in tester shows the result with its lamps.

head: Plug-in tester shows
What it means
What to do
rows: Open ground
No ground connection at the receptacle
Do not use the outlet; find the break in the EGC or the loose terminal
Hot and neutral reversed
Wired the wrong way round
Remake the connections: appliance parts can stay live when 'off'
Hot and ground reversed
A dangerous wiring error: the ground is live
Isolate at once and correct it
Open neutral or open hot
A conductor is not connected
Isolate and find the loose or broken conductor

blocks.p: Where the installation has its own ground rod, its resistance to the general mass of earth is measured with a ground electrode tester and two temporary spikes (the fall-of-potential method), with the rod disconnected from the installation. Clamp-on testers can also be used on some systems: follow the instrument's instructions.

ul: **A single rod, pipe or plate electrode must be supplemented by another electrode unless it measures 25 Ω or less.** The second electrode is normally another rod, driven at least 1.8 m (6 ft) from the first. A rod is at least 2.4 m (8 ft) long.
Metal water piping may not be the only electrode.
To lower a high reading: drive the rod deeper, add rods spaced well apart, or use another type of electrode. Dry sand, gravel and limestone give high readings; damp soil gives low ones.

blocks.note: The rod does not carry the fault current that trips a breaker. The EGC, the main bonding jumper and the neutral back to the transformer do that. The rod helps to limit voltage on the installation during lightning and surges, and to stabilise the system voltage. Both the fault path and the electrode are needed.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Before energising, and the live tests

ol: All dead tests are complete, the results are recorded and every reading passes. Any failed circuit has been repaired and retested.
All covers, filler plates and panel doors are fitted; no loose conductors or tools are left in any box.
Every breaker is off, and every load that can be disconnected is disconnected or switched off.
Everyone on the site is told, and is clear of the panels and outlets.

The service disconnect is the only thing switched on first. A competent person then checks the voltage at the service: about 110 V from each hot conductor to neutral, and about 220 V between the two hot conductors.
Breakers are switched on one at a time, each checked before the next.

blocks.p: Live tests are done by a **competent person** after these checks. As a trainee you record and interpret the results; you do not make these measurements yourself. You must understand them well enough to judge a circuit from the numbers.

When a hot conductor touches grounded metal, the fault current flows round a loop: from the transformer along the hot conductor, through the fault, back along the **EGC** to the panel's ground bar, across the **main bonding jumper** to the neutral at the service, and along the neutral back to the transformer. The NEC requires this to be a **permanent, low-impedance path that can carry the fault current**, so that the breaker opens quickly. The earth itself is not the path. The total impedance of the loop is the **loop impedance**: an instrument may call it the earth-fault loop impedance, and may show it as Zs.

**Loop impedance at an outlet = impedance measured at the service + loop resistance of the circuit.** The **ground-fault current** is **I = V ÷ Z**, where V is the voltage to ground. On a 110/220 V supply this is **110 V**, even for a 220 V circuit, because each hot conductor is 110 V from the grounded neutral. The higher the loop impedance, the smaller the fault current and the slower the breaker trips.

blocks.h: Worked example: will the breaker trip at once?

ol: A circuit is 15 m of 12 AWG (3.3 mm²) with a 12 AWG EGC at 10.4 mΩ/m. Loop resistance = 15 × 10.4 = 156 mΩ, about 0.16 Ω.
The competent person measures 0.30 Ω at the service. Expected loop impedance at the outlet = 0.30 + 0.16 = 0.46 Ω.
The maker's curve for the 20 A breaker shows it is certain to trip instantly at 200 A (ten times its rating). 239 A is more than 200 A, so it trips at once.
Another way to say it: the largest loop impedance that still gives 200 A is 110 ÷ 200 = 0.55 Ω, and the circuit's 0.46 Ω is below that.

blocks.p: The current needed for an instant trip depends on the breaker. Many thermal-magnetic breakers trip instantly somewhere between about 5 and 10 times their rating. **Use the maker's trip curve** for the breaker fitted.

blocks.h: How far below the limit should the reading be?

blocks.p: The NEC gives no fixed percentage. A conductor warms up in a fault, so its resistance rises and the real fault current is lower than a cold test suggests. Many specifications ask for a margin: follow the one you are given. Treat a reading that only just passes with suspicion.

head: Result
What it means
What to do
rows: Loop impedance well below the limit
The breaker will clear a fault in time
Record it
Loop impedance above the limit
In a ground fault the breaker may not trip fast enough; metal could stay live

Look for a poor joint or a damaged EGC; retest. If it is still high, the designer decides: a larger EGC, a different breaker, or GFCI protection. Never fit a breaker with a higher rating to 'solve' it.
Loop impedance far below the expected value
A parallel ground path, such as metal conduit or bonded pipes
Note it; it does not fail the circuit

blocks.p: Current in a conductor makes a voltage drop along it. Too much drop makes motors and compressors run hot and lights dim. The NEC **recommends** (as an informational note, not a rule) a drop of no more than **3% on a branch circuit** and **5% on the feeder and branch circuit together**. The designer decides, but you should report a circuit that is well outside it.

**Voltage drop = load current × loop resistance of the run**, where the loop resistance covers the outward and return conductors. **Percentage = drop ÷ nominal voltage × 100.** Use 110 V for a 110 V circuit and 220 V for a 220 V circuit.

ol: A 110 V circuit of 12 AWG carries 14 A over 20 m. Loop resistance of the run = 20 × 10.4 = 208 mΩ = 0.208 Ω.
As a percentage: 2.9 ÷ 110 × 100 ≈ 2.6%. That is within the 3% recommendation.
3% of 110 V is 3.3 V, so the longest run at 14 A is about 3.3 ÷ (14 × 0.0104) ≈ 22 m.

blocks.p: You can also measure it: read the voltage at the panel and at the far end with the circuit loaded, and subtract.

head: Test
Expected result
rows: GFCI TEST button
The device trips and power at the outlet goes off; RESET restores it
Plug-in tester's GFCI button
The GFCI trips at once and the tester's lamps go out
Plug-in tester's lamps before the test
The pattern for correct wiring (no open ground, no reversed polarity)
AFCI breaker TEST button
The breaker trips; reset it and record the result
User's monthly check
Pressing TEST trips the device; the user then presses RESET

blocks.p: A **GFCI** compares the current in the hot and neutral conductors. If more than about 4–6 mA leaks to ground, it trips, which is fast enough to protect a person from a serious shock. An **AFCI** detects the pattern of an electrical arc, as from a damaged cable or a loose terminal, and trips before a fire starts. A GFCI that does not trip on its own TEST button must be replaced. Do not megger GFCI or AFCI electronics. Repeated tripping may point to a neutral joined to ground in the wrong place, shared neutrals or wet fittings. You may meet the word RCD on imported equipment: in Jamaica the device is a GFCI.

blocks.h: Available fault current and interrupting rating

blocks.p: At the service and at each panel, the competent person finds the **available fault current**: the largest current that could flow in a short circuit at that point. Each breaker has an **interrupting rating** (shown in kA, sometimes as AIC) and it must be at least as large as the available fault current where it is fitted. A breaker marked 10 kA on a panel with 14 kA available is a defect. Example: a loop impedance of 0.20 Ω at 110 V gives 110 ÷ 0.20 = 550 A at that point.

ul: On three-phase supplies the competent person checks the **phase rotation** at the service and at motor circuits, so motors turn the right way.

**Functional tests** are done with the supply on: every switch, disconnect, interlock, emergency stop, GFCI, AFCI, time switch, photocell and control is operated to show it works as designed. This is the last test, not the first.

sections.title: Inspecting an existing installation, and recording defects

blocks.p: Before you start, meet the client and write down: what will be inspected and tested; what will not, and why (for example cables buried in walls and floors, circuits that cannot be switched off, areas that cannot be reached); the **sample** of accessories to be opened; and the times when circuits may be isolated. Both sign it. This protects the client and you, and the report states it.

On an existing installation you need not open every accessory. Open an agreed sample, for example one in five, spread across the building. **If you find faults, enlarge the sample**: more faults are likely. If the sample keeps finding faults, inspect everything, and tell the client why the job is taking longer.

blocks.p: Each defect is written down with **what** it is, **where** it is, **which NEC rule or drawing it breaks** (if you know it), its **seriousness** and the **action** needed. The Centre's forms may use other words, but the idea is the same:

head: Seriousness
Meaning
Examples
What the inspector does
rows: **Immediate hazard**
Someone could be hurt now
Live parts that can be touched; a broken receptacle; bare conductors in reach; a generator plugged in with a two-plug lead
Tell the person in charge at once, make it safe with their agreement (for example isolate the circuit), record it
**Must correct**
Not dangerous at this moment, but would be if a fault occurred, or it breaks a safety rule of the NEC

No grounding conductor to a metal fitting; no GFCI on an outdoor or bathroom receptacle; a breaker larger than its conductors; loop impedance too high; missing bonding; a breaker with too low an interrupting rating
Record it; urgent action is needed. On new work it must be put right before the GER's approval
**Advisory**
Does not meet the current code but is not unsafe
Old panel directory; missing labels; an older type of panel still in sound condition

**Could not verify**

A circuit that could not be traced; an odd reading that could not be followed up

blocks.p: **The overall result** is **unsatisfactory** if there is any immediate hazard or must-correct item, or an item that could not be verified and may hide one. One such item makes the whole report unsatisfactory, however good the rest is. Otherwise the result is satisfactory.

The inspector recommends the interval to the next inspection. There is no single number in the NEC. It depends on the type of building and its use, the condition found, the environment, and any requirement of the owner's insurer or the GER (confirm these with your instructor). As a guide: a quiet, well-kept building can go longer between inspections; hotels, shops and offices need them regularly; kitchens, pools, workshops, farms, coastal sites and anywhere flooded need them sooner. The report also lists the circuits not tested and why.

If the client will not let you isolate a circuit with a dangerous defect, you cannot force them. Explain the danger clearly, in writing, record their refusal on the report, and tell your supervisor. Never repair the defect live to avoid switching off, and never leave without recording what you found.

head: Work
Document
rows: New installation, or a new circuit added to an existing one
Signed test record with the panel schedule, then the GER inspection and certificate
Small addition or alteration, such as one extra outlet or a replaced fitting
Test the circuit and record the results; follow the GER's rules on alterations, and ask if you are unsure
Inspection of an existing installation
Inspection report with defects by seriousness, an overall result and a recommended next date

ul: **Inspection checklist**: each item inspected, ticked as satisfactory, not applicable, or with a comment.

**Test results**: for each circuit, its description, conductor sizes, breaker type and rating, trip current; the measured loop resistance, insulation resistance, polarity, loop impedance, GFCI and AFCI results, voltage drop where measured, and remarks. Plus the loop impedance at the service, the available fault current, the ground electrode resistance and the instruments' serial numbers.
Every reading is recorded as measured, with its unit. If a reading was not taken, say so and why.

blocks.p: The licensed electrician signs to say the work was inspected and tested and the results are true. A signature says 'I am responsible for this part and it meets the code'. Never sign for work you did not do or check.

blocks.note: After a repair, the circuit is **retested** and the new results recorded. Never copy results from another circuit, and never record a circuit as tested when it was not. A false record is fraud, and it can put a life at risk.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Explain the results to the client in plain words
Show them the GFCI and AFCI TEST buttons and how often to press them
Give them the signed test record, the panel schedule and any report
Point out the panel directory and the labels
Explain each defect and what must be done, with a written quotation where asked
Record the handover with signatures and dates

blocks.h: The GER inspection and JPS connection

blocks.p: For a new or altered installation in Jamaica, the contractor completes the verification and test record first. The **GER** then arranges the inspection against the NEC and the approved drawings, and a licensed inspector certifies it. If it passes, the approval allows **JPS** to connect or reconnect the supply. Keep a copy of every record and approval for the client and for your own files.

blocks.note: Which forms are used, who may certify, and what an alteration needs are set by the GER and may change. Your instructor will confirm the current procedure for the Centre.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

terms: Advisory
A defect that does not meet the current code but is not unsafe; the client should plan to deal with it.
AFCI
Arc-fault circuit interrupter: a device that trips when it detects dangerous arcing.
Available fault current
The largest current that could flow in a short circuit or ground fault at a point.
Defect report
The written list of what is wrong, where, how serious it is and the action needed.
Equipment grounding conductor (EGC)
The conductor run with the circuit that carries ground-fault current back to the panel.
Effective ground-fault current path
The low-impedance path that lets a ground fault trip the breaker quickly.
Extent and limitations
The written agreement of what an inspection will and will not cover.
Fire-stopping
Material that seals openings where cables pass through fire-rated walls and floors.
Functional test
Operating switches, controls, GFCIs and interlocks with the supply on, to show they work.
GER
The Government Electrical Regulator, which replaced the Government Electrical Inspectorate and oversees inspection and approval.
GFCI
Ground-fault circuit interrupter: trips at about 4–6 mA of leakage to protect people.
Immediate hazard
A defect that could hurt someone now; it is made safe at once.
Initial verification
Inspection and testing of a new installation or addition before it is used.
Interrupting rating
The largest fault current a breaker can safely interrupt.
Loop impedance
The total impedance of the path a ground fault takes from hot conductor to ground and back to the source; some instruments call it earth-fault loop impedance.
Main bonding jumper
The connection at the service that joins the neutral, the grounding conductors and the service equipment together.
Must correct
A defect that would become dangerous if a fault occurred, or that breaks a safety rule; urgent action.
NEMA enclosure type
A US rating of an enclosure's protection, such as 3R or 4X.
Panel schedule
The list of circuits with their conductor sizes, lengths, breakers and what they feed.
Polarity
Correct connection of hot, neutral and ground, with switches and breakers in the hot conductor.
Sampling
Opening and checking a part of the accessories to stand for all of them, enlarged if faults are found.
Service
The point where the supply enters the building and the main disconnect is fitted.
Voltage drop
The voltage lost along a conductor when current flows.

c1.title: A new villa at Duncans
c1.text: Shauna, a Level 3 trainee, leads two Level 2 trainees on the initial verification of a new villa at Duncans, Trelawny. The JPS supply is 110/220 V. The competent person measures the loop impedance at the service as 0.28 Ω. The outdoor receptacle circuit is 24 m of 14 AWG (2.1 mm²) hot conductor with a 14 AWG grounding conductor, which the cable data gives as 16.6 mΩ per metre for the pair. It is fed by a 15 A breaker, and the maker's curve shows it trips instantly at 150 A. A trainee reports the loop resistance of the circuit as 1.45 Ω.

c2.title: An inspection at a Santa Cruz pharmacy
c2.text: Mr Fenton owns a pharmacy in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, in a building wired about twenty-five years ago. He asks for an inspection but says that one refrigerator circuit, holding vaccines, cannot be switched off at all. The team agrees to open one accessory in five. On the staff-room wall there is a receptacle whose broken faceplate leaves the terminals exposed, and the rear store has an added air-conditioning circuit of 12 AWG (3.3 mm²) conductors on a 40 A breaker.

c3.title: Insulation tests at a Mandeville call centre
c3.text: A call centre in Mandeville, Manchester, has had a new floor wired with fourteen receptacle circuits, each feeding computer workstations with surge protective devices in the floor boxes. Tested together at the panel, the circuits read 0.39 MΩ at 500 V DC. Tested one at a time, thirteen circuits read 200 MΩ or more and one reads 0.4 MΩ. On a separate panel, a 24 V DC circuit for the door-entry system also needs testing.

c4.title: A generator at a Port Maria guest house
c4.text: A guest house in Port Maria, St Mary, has fitted a 12 kVA petrol generator on the back veranda, under the kitchen window. The owner's handyman connected it by a lead with a plug at each end: one end goes into the generator's outlet and the other into a 220 V dryer receptacle in the laundry, and the owner switches off the main breaker 'before starting it'. The team is asked to inspect the installation and to advise.

c5.title: Grounding and GFCI checks at a Linstead clinic
c5.text: Marlon, a Level 3 trainee, supervises Level 2 trainees testing a new clinic in Linstead, St Catherine. The service has one 2.4 m ground rod, and a competent person measures it at 38 Ω by the fall-of-potential method. In a treatment room, a trainee's plug-in tester shows 'open ground' on one receptacle. In the bathroom, the plug-in tester's GFCI button trips the GFCI receptacle, but the receptacle's own TEST button does nothing.

questions.q: What loop resistance should Shauna expect for the outdoor receptacle circuit from the cable data?
o: About 4.0 Ω
About 0.40 Ω
About 0.040 Ω
About 0.80 Ω
questions.why: 24 m × 16.6 mΩ/m = 398.4 mΩ, which is about 0.40 Ω. The trainee's 1.45 Ω is more than three times that, so something is wrong: a test error, a loose joint, a damaged grounding conductor or a longer route than drawn.

questions.q: Using the expected loop resistance, what ground-fault current should flow at the far end, and does it reach the 150 A needed?
o: About 275 A: yes, and with a large margin to spare
About 102 A: no, it falls short of the 150 A needed
About 162 A: yes, but with only a small margin
About 393 A: yes, and with a very large margin to spare
questions.why: Loop impedance = 0.28 + 0.40 = 0.68 Ω, so I = 110 ÷ 0.68 ≈ 162 A, above 150 A. The margin is small, and conductors warm up in a fault and their resistance rises, so the designer should be told. Forgetting the 0.28 Ω gives 275 A; doubling the circuit's 0.40 Ω gives 102 A.

questions.q: If the circuit's loop resistance really were 1.45 Ω, about what ground-fault current would flow, and would the breaker trip instantly?
o: About 76 A: no, it needs 150 A to trip instantly
About 64 A: no, it needs 150 A to trip instantly
About 64 A: yes, because that is above its 15 A rating
About 275 A: yes, it is well above 150 A
questions.why: Loop impedance = 0.28 + 1.45 = 1.73 Ω, and I = 110 ÷ 1.73 ≈ 64 A, well below the 150 A needed. The breaker would trip only on its slow thermal element, if at all, and metalwork could stay live. The circuit must not be energised until the fault is found.

questions.q: The trainee's reading of 1.45 Ω is far above the expected value. What should Shauna do first?
o: Record 1.45 Ω and pass the circuit, as it is still under 2 Ω
Record the expected 0.40 Ω instead, since the cable data is reliable
Change the breaker to 10 A so that less fault current is needed
Check the leads were nulled and the method, then retest it herself
questions.why: A reading far above expectation is either a test error (leads not nulled, poor probe contact, wrong points) or a real defect. Check the method and retest. If it is still high, look for a loose joint or damaged conductor. Never record a value that was not measured.

questions.q: How should the vaccine refrigerator circuit be handled in the inspection?
o: Switch it off briefly, since vaccines keep for an hour
Test it live, as safety matters more than the vaccines
Move the vaccines to the staff room and test it quietly
Record it as not tested, and say why in the report
questions.why: What cannot be tested is agreed with the client and written into the extent and limitations, and the report says it was not verified and why. Switching off or moving the vaccines without agreement could spoil them, and working live is not an option.

questions.q: What should the team recommend for the air-conditioning circuit?
o: Fit a 60 A breaker so that it never trips in use
Leave it alone, since the unit has worked for years
Have the circuit sized to the unit's nameplate
Add a GFCI breaker and keep the same conductors
questions.why: The breaker and conductors must be matched to the unit's nameplate and the NEC, and 12 AWG cannot be protected at 40 A. A bigger breaker makes it worse, and a GFCI does not protect conductors from overload. The designer or the licensed electrician must size it, and it must meet the GER's rules for alterations.

questions.q: How should the receptacle with exposed terminals and the air-conditioning circuit each be recorded?
o: Receptacle: immediate hazard; air conditioner: immediate hazard
Receptacle: immediate hazard; air conditioner: must correct
Receptacle: must correct; air conditioner: must correct
Receptacle: must correct; air conditioner: advisory
questions.why: Exposed live terminals can hurt someone now: immediate hazard, made safe at once with the client's agreement. A 12 AWG circuit on a 40 A breaker is not dangerous this minute but would overheat in an overload: must correct. Either item makes the overall result unsatisfactory.

questions.q: Mr Fenton asks how soon the next inspection should be. Which answer is best?
o: Ten years, the same as for any ordinary house
A date based on its age, use and condition found
Never, because the GER approved it when it was built
One month, because the exposed receptacle was found
questions.why: The NEC gives no single interval. The inspector recommends one on the report from the type of use, the age, the condition found and the environment, and any rule of the owner's insurer or the GER. Unfixed defects, a damp or coastal site and heavy use all make it sooner.

questions.q: Why is the whole-panel reading of 0.39 MΩ so much lower than thirteen of the single circuits?
o: The surge devices raise the reading of each circuit on its own
The tester's battery was low during the combined test
The panel's main breaker must have been left closed
Circuits in parallel read lower, and one circuit is very low
questions.why: Insulation resistances combine like parallel resistors, so a panel reads lower than any single circuit, and one very low circuit pulls the total down towards its own value. Thirteen circuits at 200 MΩ or more and one at 0.4 MΩ give about 0.39 MΩ. A low whole-panel reading is a prompt to test each circuit alone.

questions.q: What should be done about the circuit reading 0.4 MΩ?
o: Record it as a pass, since the other thirteen circuits read well
Energise it and see whether the breaker trips
Disconnect its surge device and equipment, then retest it
Fit a GFCI to it, since a GFCI covers low insulation readings
questions.why: Surge protective devices and electronic equipment make insulation readings false and can be damaged by the test. Disconnect them and retest. If the circuit still reads below the limit the specification gives (typically 1 MΩ), find the fault by splitting the circuit. It cannot be passed or energised until it is found.

questions.q: What should the team do before testing the 24 V DC door-entry circuit with the insulation tester?
o: Test it at 1 000 V to prove the cable is really sound
Leave its electronics connected so they are tested as well
Disconnect its electronics and use the maker's test voltage
Skip the test, as low-voltage circuits cannot have any faults
questions.why: A 500 V test can destroy door-entry electronics and gives a false reading through them. Disconnect the electronics and follow the maker's instructions for the test voltage. Low-voltage cable can still be damaged, so the circuit is still tested.

questions.q: What is the most serious danger of the two-plug lead arrangement?
o: With the main on, the generator would back-feed JPS lines
The generator will run short of fuel on long outages
The dryer receptacle's breaker will trip when the generator runs
The generator's engine will run too fast with no load
questions.why: Nothing stops the generator and the mains being connected together except the owner remembering to switch off. If the main breaker is on, the generator feeds the JPS lines through the service transformer, at high voltage, and can kill a line worker. The prongs of the lead are also live when it is plugged into the generator.

questions.q: Which arrangement should the team recommend?
o: A sign on the main breaker reminding the owner to switch it off first
A heavier lead with plugs on both ends, to carry the full current
An interlocked transfer switch, with a proper generator inlet
A second main breaker beside the first, so that both can be switched
questions.why: A transfer switch, interlocked so that the generator and mains can never be connected together, with a proper generator inlet and cable, is the safe arrangement. The generator must also be moved away from the kitchen window because of carbon monoxide, be grounded as designed, and a dual-supply warning label put at the panel.

questions.q: How should the present generator connection be recorded in the inspection report?
o: Advisory, as generators are common in Jamaica
Immediate hazard: remove the lead with the owner's agreement
Not recorded, as the generator is not part of the fixed wiring
Must correct, to be put right at the next inspection
questions.why: A back-feed and live prongs could hurt someone now, so it is an immediate hazard. The inspector tells the owner at once, makes it safe with their agreement by removing the lead, records it, and gives the overall result as unsatisfactory.

questions.q: The single ground rod measures 38 Ω. What should happen next?
o: Nothing: a single rod is accepted at any reading
A second electrode, at least 1.8 m from the first, is added
The grounding electrode conductor is replaced with a thinner one
The rod is painted to cut its resistance
questions.why: A single rod, pipe or plate electrode must be supplemented by another unless it measures 25 Ω or less. 38 Ω is above that, so a second electrode (usually another rod, at least 1.8 m from the first) is added. The system is then accepted without a further measurement, although a retest is good practice.

questions.q: The plug-in tester shows 'open ground' on a treatment-room receptacle. What does this mean?
o: The hot and neutral are reversed at the receptacle terminals
The receptacle has no connection to the ground conductor
The GFCI upstream of the receptacle has tripped open
The voltage at the receptacle is too low for the load
questions.why: 'Open ground' means there is no ground connection at the receptacle: the EGC is broken, missing or not connected at the terminal. It must be found and repaired before the outlet is used, and the circuit's continuity retested.

questions.q: The tester's button trips the bathroom GFCI, but its own TEST button does nothing. What should Marlon do?
o: Accept it, because the tester trips it
Replace it, as the TEST button must also work
Paint over the TEST button so users do not press it
Fit an AFCI beside it and leave it in place
questions.why: A GFCI must trip on its own TEST button, because the user will rely on that button. A device that fails either check is replaced and the new one tested. A working tester result does not excuse a dead button.

questions.q: At a panel the competent person finds an available fault current of 14 kA. The breakers fitted are marked 10 kA interrupting rating. How should this be recorded?
o: Satisfactory, since 10 kA is the usual rating for breakers
Satisfactory, as the fault current falls to zero once the breaker trips
A defect: the breakers cannot safely interrupt this fault current
A note to fit larger conductors, which will lower the fault current
questions.why: A breaker's interrupting rating must be at least the available fault current where it is fitted; otherwise a big fault could burst it. 10 kA breakers on a 14 kA panel are a defect, usually must correct. Larger conductors would raise the fault current, not lower it.

questions.q: A 220 V pump circuit uses 10 AWG (5.3 mm²) conductors, 45 m long, at 6.6 mΩ per metre for the pair of hot conductors. It carries 20 A. What is the voltage drop, and how does it compare with the 3% recommendation?
o: About 5.9 V, or 2.7%: within the recommendation
About 5.9 V, or 5.4%: over the recommendation
About 11.9 V, or 5.4%: over the recommendation
About 3.0 V, or 1.4%: well within the recommendation
questions.why: Voltage drop = 20 A × (45 m × 6.6 mΩ/m) = 20 × 0.297 Ω ≈ 5.9 V. On a 220 V circuit, 5.9 ÷ 220 × 100 ≈ 2.7%, which is within 3%. Using 110 V as the base wrongly gives 5.4%.

questions.q: At a receptacle in a store, the plug-in tester shows hot and neutral reversed. Why does this matter?
o: Appliance parts stay live when they are switched off
The appliance will run at half its rated voltage
The breaker will trip the moment anything is plugged in
The insulation resistance of the circuit will read too low
questions.why: With reversed polarity, an appliance's switch or fuse breaks the neutral instead of the hot conductor, so its internal parts and a lamp's screw shell stay live when it is 'off'. Someone repairing it could be shocked. Remake the connections and retest.
